domain: International Relations / International Law / Political Economy
topic_summary: Analysis of the contested nature of the Rules-Based International Order (RBIO), examining whether it represents a neutral coordination framework or an extractive hegemonic structure. The topic centers on how different state actors interpret the legitimacy, universality, and amendability of post-WWII international norms and institutions.

key_entities: United States (post-WWII architect; primary norm enforcer)
United Nations Security Council (primary legitimation mechanism)
Bretton Woods Institutions (IMF/World Bank; economic governance)
Global South states (heterogeneous coalition; mixed dependency/resentment)
key_tensions: Universality claim vs selective enforcement (humanitarian intervention; ICC jurisdiction)
Sovereignty protection vs intervention authority (R2P doctrine; sanctions regimes)
Amendment impossibility vs functional obsolescence (UNSC veto; treaty revision deadlock)
key_mechanisms: UNSC P5 veto (grants 5 states absolute blocking authority)
Conditionality lending (IMF structural adjustment; World Bank project criteria)
Norm entrepreneurship (humanitarian intervention precedents; atrocity prevention)
key_absences: Formal amendment process for core UN Charter provisions beyond Article 108/109
Binding dispute resolution for great power conflicts (UNSC deadlock endemic)
Representation mechanisms for post-colonial states in governance design

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The uncodified practice-norm complex of post-1945 international order: state sovereignty, territorial integrity, peaceful dispute resolution, and free trade/capital flows as mutually reinforcing and universally applicable
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Interpretive legitimacy claimed through: (1) consent-based treaty law (UN Charter Article 2); (2) customary international law derived from state practice; (3) enforcement capacity via UNSC authorization and U.S.-led coalitions
commitment_system_recognition.candidate_pattern: dual_sovereignty (state sovereignty as kernel commitment; competing claims about who legitimately interprets exceptions)

readings.commitment: RBIO norms are universal, consent-based, and revisable through legitimate multilateral processes; enforcement selectivity is a capacity problem, not a legitimacy problem
readings.authority_grounding: Democratic peace theory; consent-based treaty law; track record of conflict reduction vs pre-1945 era
readings.expected_structural_delta: Intervention justified when UNSC authorizes or grave atrocities occur; economic conditionality acceptable as contract terms; beneficiary: intervening states and their contractors; victim: targeted states and their civilian populations during sanctions

readings.commitment: RBIO norms are a frozen hegemonic project: formally revisable but practically un-amendable due to P5 veto and institutional path-dependency; enforcement selectivity reveals extractive intent
readings.authority_grounding: Historical materialism; dependency theory; empirical record of selective enforcement (Iraq 2003 vs Chechnya; Libya vs Yemen)
readings.expected_structural_delta: Any intervention not authorized by target state is illegitimate; conditionality is coerced contract; beneficiary: U.S. and European capital; victim: Global South states and populations subjected to structural adjustment

readings.commitment: State sovereignty is absolute; RBIO norms legitimate only when they protect sovereignty against external interference; humanitarian exceptions are pretexts for regime change
readings.authority_grounding: Westphalian sovereignty; UN Charter Article 2(7) (non-intervention); post-colonial state formation experience
readings.expected_structural_delta: No legitimate intervention authority beyond self-defense; conditionality acceptable only when target state can exit without cost; beneficiary: authoritarian regimes; victim: populations trapped under repressive governments with no external recourse

axiom_contradictions.basis: Liberal reading holds multilateral institutions CAN legitimately override sovereignty when authorized; hegemonic reading holds such authorization is itself structurally illegitimate due to frozen power distribution. No framework can hold both: either authorization process is legitimate or it is not.

Liberal reading accepts humanitarian intervention as legitimate exception to sovereignty; sovereignty maximalist reading holds sovereignty admits no exceptions. One requires accepting that external actors can legitimately judge internal affairs; the other categorically denies this.

Hegemonic reading accepts intervention could be legitimate if power distribution were equitable; sovereignty maximalist reading rejects intervention categorically regardless of who authorizes it. These are different foundational commitments about whether any external authority can ever override sovereignty.

omegas.description: Are these three genuine readings of one kernel, or three separate kernels masquerading as one? If sovereignty protection and free trade/capital flows are separable commitments with different historical trajectories, the kernel may fracture under analysis.

Global South states do not form a coherent bloc: some align with sovereignty maximalism (Russia-China), others with conditional liberalism (conditional on reform). Treating them as single victim/beneficiary set may obscure intra-South extraction dynamics.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory): representation mechanisms

omegas.description: Is the order genuinely un-amendable, or are alternative institutions (AIIB, BRICS+) constituting de facto amendment through competitive governance? If exit + build alternative is viable, hegemonic_extraction_reading's claimed lock-in weakens.

Do humanitarian interventions systematically produce worse outcomes than non-intervention? Outcome data (Libya post-2011, Iraq post-2003) bears on whether liberal_institutional_reading's capacity framing holds or collapses into extraction.
omegas.source: F03 concern: liberal_institutional_reading may assume universal applicability without outcome evidence

omegas.description: Are sanctions effective coercion or performative signaling? If target states durably resist (Russia post-2022, Iran post-2012), the snare classification may overstate extractive yield.

fracture_scan.notes: F03 detected: liberal_institutional_reading assumes universal applicability and revisability through legitimate processes, but amendment mechanisms (Article 108/109) have never successfully reformed core governance structures. Generated omega_intervention_outcomes and omega_revision_mechanisms to bound this uncertainty. All three readings rest on contested empirical claims about enforcement patterns that training data may not adjudicate reliably.
